Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verse 1–4:

﴿These are the verses of the Book and a manifest Qur'an.﴾ It is possible that he means by "the Book" the earlier scriptures, and that "and a Qur'an" is coordinated with them; but the apparent meaning is that it refers to the Qur'an itself, and its coordination is the coordination of attributes.

﴿Perhaps﴾ (rubama) is read with both the light and the heavy pronunciation, and both are dialects. The word "ma" is a particle that prevents "rubba" (perhaps/many a) from governing what follows. The meaning of "rubba" is diminution (fewness), though it may also be used for abundance. It has been said that this usage is of that kind; and it has been said that the expression of abundance by a particle of fewness is like His saying: ﴿We see the turning of your face toward the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144], and ﴿He knows what you are upon﴾ [al-Nur: 64]. It has also been said that the sense of fewness in this verse is that if they wished to embrace Islam even once, they ought to hasten to it; how much more so when they wish it many times over. "Rubba" is only used with the past tense.

﴿The ones who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾. It has been said that this is at the time of death; it has been said that it is on the Day of Resurrection; and it has been said that it is when the disobedient Muslims come out of the Fire. This last is the more preferred view, because of a hadith narrated on this matter.

﴿Leave them﴾ and what follows it is a threat. ﴿A decreed term﴾: that is, a limited time.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verses 6–8:

﴿And they say, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman."﴾ The pronoun in "they say" refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. Their saying "to whom the Reminder has been sent down" is meant in a mocking manner, i.e., "according to your claim and assertion."

﴿"Why do you not bring us the angels?"﴾ Lawla mā (why not / if only ... not) is used here for urging and reproach. The meaning is that they asked the Prophet ﷺ to bring the angels along with him.

﴿"We do not send down the angels except with truth."﴾ This is a response to what they proposed. The meaning is that the angels do not descend except with truth, namely revelation and the interests that Allah intends, not by the proposal of one who proposes or the choice of a disbeliever. It has also been said that "the truth" here means punishment.

﴿And they would not have been granted respite.﴾ Idhan (then, in that case) is a particle of response and consequence. The meaning is: had the angels been sent down, the punishment of these disbelievers who proposed their descent would not have been delayed, because it is Allah's custom that whoever proposes a sign, sees it, and does not believe, is hastened to punishment. Yet Allah knew that many of these people would believe, and their descendants would believe, so He did not do that to them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verses 9–12:

﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians.﴾ *Al-dhikr* (the Reminder) here refers to the Qur'an. In His words ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾ is a rebuttal of their denial and their mockery in their saying ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are surely mad﴾. For this reason He emphasised it with *nahnu* ("We"), and He argued for it by His preservation of it. The meaning of its preservation (*hifz*) is its safeguarding from alteration and change, as happened to other scriptures. God took upon Himself the preservation of the Qur'an, so no one is able to add to it or subtract from it, or change it. This differs from other books, whose preservation was entrusted to their own people, as in His words ﴿for they were charged with the preservation of the Book of God﴾ (al-Ma'ida: 44).

﴿among the sects of the ancients.﴾ *Al-shiya'* is the plural of *shi'a*, which is a group that follows a school of thought or a man.

﴿Thus We cause it to enter into the hearts of the guilty.﴾ The meaning of *naslukuhu* ("We cause it to enter") is "We make it enter." The pronoun in *naslukuhu* may refer to the mockery, which is indicated by His words ﴿they mock at it﴾, or it may refer to the Qur'an, meaning "We cause it to enter their hearts so that they mock at it." In the latter case, His words ﴿thus﴾ serve as a comparison to the mockery mentioned earlier. His words ﴿they do not believe in it﴾ explain the reason for its entering their hearts, and the pronoun in *bihi* ("in it") refers to the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verses 13–15:

﴿And the way of the former peoples has already passed (before them)﴾. That is, their course had gone before in this state of disbelief and mockery, until they were destroyed because of it. So in the statement there is a warning to Quraysh.

﴿And even if We opened for them a gate from the heaven, and they continued to ascend through it, they would surely say: "Our eyes have only been intoxicated (sukkirat)."﴾ The pronouns refer to the stubborn disbelievers of Quraysh, who are destined to disbelief. It has also been said: the pronoun in "zallu" (they continued) and in "ya'rujun" (they ascend) refers to the angels, and the pronoun in "qalu" (they said) refers to the disbelievers. The meaning of "ya'rujun" is "yasʿadun" (they ascend). The sense is that these disbelievers, even if they saw the greatest sign, would say: it is mere imagination (takhyil) or sorcery. It is also read as "sukkirat" with shaddah and without shaddah. It may be derived from al-sukr (intoxication), so its meaning would be: our eyes have been compelled, so we saw the matter other than as it really is; or it may be derived from al-sikr, which means blocking (al-sadd), so its meaning would be: our eyes have been prevented from seeing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verses 21–22:

﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries﴾. It was said: this means rain, though the wording is more general than that. The word "khaza'in" (treasuries) refers to the places where things are stored. The apparent meaning of this is that things already exist, having been created. It was also said that this is a figure of speech, and the meaning is: there is not a thing but that We are able to bring it into existence and form it, ﴿in a known measure﴾, i.e., in a specific, limited quantity. ﴿And We send the winds fertilizing﴾. It is said: the she-camel and the tree "laqihat" (became pregnant/fruitful) when they conceived, so she is "laqih" (pregnant), and the wind "alqahat" (fertilized) the trees, so they are "mulqah" (fertilized). "Lawaqih" is the plural of "laqih", because the wind carries water, or it is the plural of "mulqihah" with the extra letter "mim" dropped.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verse 24–26:

﴿And We certainly know those who go forward [among you], and We certainly know those who lag behind.﴾ The verse: it means the first and the last of mankind. This is mentioned as evidence for the gathering (al-hashr) mentioned afterwards in His words: ﴿Indeed, your Lord – it is He who will gather them.﴾ For when He encompasses them in knowledge, their re-creation and gathering are not difficult for Him. It is also said: it means those who go forward in birth and death, and those who come later. It is also said: those who went forward to Islam and those who lagged behind it. ﴿And We certainly created man from clay of dried mud (ṣalṣāl) [that is] from black mud altered (ḥama'in masnūn).﴾ "Al-insān" here is Ādam, peace be upon him. Ṣalṣāl: dried clay that rings (yuṣalṣilu), i.e., makes a sound, and it is unfired; when it is fired, it becomes pottery (fakhkhār). ﴿from black mud altered⁠ (ḥama'in masnūn)⁠﴾ Ḥama': black clay. Masnūn: that which has changed and become foul-smelling. It is also said: it derives from asana, when it changes; but morphology (al-taṣrīf) refutes this view. The phrase "min ḥama'in" is a description (ṣifa) of ṣalṣāl: i.e., ṣalṣāl existing from ḥama'.

Then go out from it (ﷺ... no) — let me translate carefully.

**"So go out from it"** — i.e., from the Garden, or from the heavens.

**"He said: My Lord"** — this implies his acknowledgment of Lordship (rubūbiyyah), and that his disbelief was in a manner other than denial, namely his objection against God in His command to prostrate to Adam.

**"Until the day of the appointed time"** — the day that Iblis asked to be respited until is the Day of Resurrection. Iblis's request to be respited until the Day of Resurrection was ignorance on his part and sophistry, for he asked for something that could not be attained. Had he been given what he asked, he would never have died, since no one dies after the Resurrection. So when he asked for what could not be attained, God turned away from him and granted him respite until the first blast.

**﴿Because You have led me astray⦆** The bāʾ (ب) here indicates causation (sababiyya): meaning, "I will mislead them because of Your misleading me." It was also said that it is an oath, as if he said: "By Your power to mislead me, I will mislead them." The pronoun refers to the descendants of Adam.

**﴿He said: "This is a path that leads straight to Me."﴾** The one who says this is Allah, exalted is He. The reference of "this" (hādhā) is to the salvation of the sincere servants from Iblis, and that he has no power over them; or it refers to the division of people into those who are misguided (ghawī) and those who are sincere (mukhlaṣ).

**﴿except Your servants﴾** It is necessary that by "servants" (ʿibād) is meant all people, so that His saying, "except those who follow you," is an exception of the connected type (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), meaning that by "servants" He means the sincere ones; in that case the exception is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ).

**﴿And indeed Hell is their promised place﴾** The pronoun refers to the misguided ones (al-ghāwūn).

**﴿It has seven gates﴾** It is related that it consists of seven levels (aṭbāq), each level having a gate. The uppermost is for the sinful among the Muslims; the second is for the Jews; the third is for the Christians; the fourth is for the Ṣābiʾa (Sabians); the fifth is for the Magians (Majūs); the sixth is for the polytheists; and the seventh is for the hypocrites.

**﴿Enter it; peace⦆** The implied sense is that it will be said to them: "Enter it." The word "peace" (al-salām) may mean greeting (al-taḥiyya) or safety (al-salāma).

**﴿as brothers﴾** This means brotherhood of affection and faith.

**﴿facing one another﴾** That is, each of them faces the others on couches (ʿalā al-asira).

**﴿fatigue (naṣab)﴾** That is, toil or weariness.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verse 49–56:

﴿Inform My servants﴾ (the verse): I inform them. The verse is one of hope (tarjiyah) and fear (takhwif).

﴿And inform them about the guests of Ibrahim﴾. "Guest" (ḍayf) here refers to a group, namely the angels who came to Ibrahim (Abraham) with glad tidings.

﴿They were afraid﴾ (wajilun), i.e., fearful; wajal means fear.

﴿Do not fear﴾ (lā tawjal), i.e., do not be afraid.

﴿Indeed, We give you glad tidings of a boy with much knowledge﴾: he is Ishaq (Isaac).

﴿He said: "Do you give me glad tidings of a child when old age has touched me?"﴾ The meaning is: you give me glad tidings of a child although my years have advanced. At that time he was one hundred years old, and it was said: more.

﴿Then for what do you give glad tidings?﴾ He said this in a manner of wonder at his having a child in his old age, or in a manner of considering it unlikely. "He said, 'Then what is your business, O messengers?'" That is, what is your affair, and for what reason have you come? ﴿To a people who are criminals﴾, meaning the people of Lot. ﴿Except the family of Lot﴾. This may be an exception from "the people of Lot," in which case it is disjunctive (munqati'), since it describes the people as criminals while the family of Lot were not criminals. It may also be an exception from the pronoun in "criminals," in which case it is connected (muttasil), as if he had said: "To a people who have all committed crime, except the family of Lot, for they did not commit it." ﴿Except his wife﴾: this is an exception from "the family of Lot," so it is an exception from an exception. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an exception from the pronoun in the phrase of the angels, "[We] will deliver them," and this is what the meaning requires. ﴿We have decreed that she is among those who remain behind﴾. Al-Ghabir is used to mean "the one who remains" and also "the one who departs." The angels attributed the act of decreeing to themselves, although it belongs to God alone, because of their nearness and special standing with God, especially in this matter, just as the close companion of a king says to the king, "We have arranged such-and-such." It may also be that this is a report from God. ﴿A people unknown [to us]﴾, that is, we do not know them. ﴿They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they used to doubt"﴾, that is, we have brought you the punishment for your people. Yamtarun means they were in doubt about it. ﴿And follow behind them﴾, that is, be behind them, at the rear of their column, until none of them is left behind, and so that they walk in front of him; then his heart will not be occupied with them, for if they were behind him he would be anxious for them. ﴿And let not any of you look back﴾, which was discussed in Hud. ﴿And proceed to where you are commanded﴾. It was said: it is Egypt. It was also said: "where" here refers to time, since no place was mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verses 71–76:

﴿He said, "These are my daughters"﴾ He invited them to marry his daughters so that he might protect his guests thereby.

﴿By your life﴾ An oath; "al-'umr" means life. In this there is an honour for the Prophet ﷺ, that Allah swore by his life. It was also said that this is from the words of the angels to Lot, and its subject (mubtada') is in the nominative, with its predicate (khabar) omitted, its estimated form being: "By your life, my oath." The lam is the lam of preparation (lam al-tawti'ah).

﴿Indeed, they were in their intoxication, wandering blindly﴾ The pronoun refers to the people of Lot. Their intoxication (sakrah) is their misguidance and ignorance, and "ya'mahun" means they are bewildered.

﴿So the Shout seized them﴾ That is, the shout of Gabriel, which was his seizing of them.

﴿at sunrise﴾ That is, entering into the time of sunrise (shuruq), which is the time of the sun's rising. The explanation of what follows of their story has already been given in Hud [11:76].

﴿for those who discern﴾ That is, for those who read signs (mutafarrisin), and from it comes the insight (firasah) of the believer. It was also said: for those who take lessons (mu'tabirin). The reality of tawassum is looking at the mark (simah).

﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains﴾ That is, on a path that is established and seen by people. The pronoun refers to the destroyed city.

﴿And indeed, the companions of the Thicket were certainly wrongdoers﴾. The companions of the Thicket (Aṣḥāb al-Aykah) were the people of Shu'ayb, and al-Aykah is a dense thicket of trees. When they disbelieved, God set it ablaze over them as a fire.

﴿the messengers﴾: He used the plural, although they denied only one of them. There are two interpretations of this. The second is that he meant the category as a whole, like your saying, "So-and-so rides horses," even if he has only ridden one horse.

﴿secure﴾: That is, secure from their houses collapsing, because of how solid they were. It is also said: secure from the punishment of God.

﴿except with truth﴾: That is, they were not created in vain.

﴿except with truth﴾: That is, they were not created in vain.

﴿So turn away with gracious forgiveness﴾: It is said that gracious forgiveness (al-safh al-jamil) is that which is free of punishment and rebuke. In this verse there is a truce with the disbelievers, which was abrogated (naskh) by the sword.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 15, verse 87:**

﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses]﴾ (al-mathani, the oft-repeated verses). He means: Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an), because it consists of seven verses. It was also said: he means the seven long surahs, which are al-Baqarah, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'idah, al-An'am, al-A'raf, and al-Anfal together with Bara'ah. The first view is more likely (arjah), because it is reported in the hadith. The word al-mathani is derived from al-tathniyah, which means repetition, because al-Fatihah is repeated in recitation in the prayer, and because other surahs contain repeated narratives and other material. It was also said that it is derived from al-thana' (praise), because it contains praise of God. The particle min may be partitive (lil-tab'id) or explanatory (li-bayan al-jins). The conjunction of "the Qur'an" with "the seven oft-repeated [verses]" is because it refers to what is other than them of the Qur'an, so it is a general term after a specific one ('umum ba'da khusus).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verses 88–90:

﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾ meaning: do not look at what We have given them to enjoy in this world. It is as if He says: We have given you the seven oft-repeated (al-sab' al-mathani) and the mighty Qur'an, so do not look at the world, for what We have given you is far greater than it. ﴿Pairs of them﴾ meaning categories of disbelievers. ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ meaning do not be distressed by their disbelief. ﴿And lower your wing﴾ meaning be humble and gentle ﴿to the believers﴾. The "wing" here is a metaphor. ﴿As We sent down upon the dividers﴾. The kaf in kama (as) is connected to His words "I am the warner," meaning: I warn Quraysh of a punishment like the punishment that was sent down upon the dividers (al-muqtasimin). It was also said that it is connected to His words "And We have certainly given you," meaning: We have sent down to you a Book as We sent down to the dividers. There is disagreement about the dividers (al-muqtasimin). It was said: they are the People of the Book who believed in part of their Book and disbelieved in part of it, so they divided themselves into two parts. It was also said: they are Quraysh, who divided the gates of Makkah during the season (of pilgrimage), each of them standing at a gate; one of them would say, "He is a poet," another would say, "He is a sorcerer," and so on.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verses 91–93:

﴿Those who made the Qur'an into 'iḍīn (fragments)﴾. Meaning: parts. They said various things about it. The singular of ʿiḍīn is ʿiḍah. It was also said that it derives from al-ʿaḍh (ʿaḍhah), which means sorcery, and that al-ʿāḍih is the sorcerer. The meaning according to this view is that it is sorcery. The word is defective in its lam: its lam is a waw according to the first opinion, and a hāʾ according to the second.

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾. If it is asked: how can this be reconciled with His saying, "On that Day, no human or jinn will be questioned about his sin"? The answer is that the affirmed questioning is in the manner of reckoning and rebuke, while the negated questioning is in the manner of pure inquiry, because Allah knows the deeds and so has no need to ask about them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 15, verses 94–99:

﴿So proclaim openly what you are commanded﴾, meaning: declare it plainly and carry it out. ﴿Indeed, We suffice you against the mockers﴾, meaning a group of the people of Mecca. Allah destroyed them by various kinds of destruction, without any effort on the part of the Prophet (ﷺ). They were five: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-'As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, and 'Adi ibn Qays. The account of their destruction is mentioned in the biographical works (al-siyar). It has also been said that they were those who were killed at Badr, such as Abu Jahl, 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, Umayya ibn Khalaf, 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt and others. The first view is more preferred (arjah), because Allah sufficed him against them in Mecca before the Hijra. ﴿And We certainly know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾, a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) and a comforting. ﴿Until there comes to you the certainty﴾, meaning death.
